paper.title: Forecasting Inequalities in Survival to Retirement Age by Socioeconomic Status in Denmark and Sweden
paper.code_data_availability: Data Availability: 'Access to individual-level data is restricted by Danish law. …

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish registries / Danish registry data
registers.role: sample frame, treatment (income-based SES) and outcomes (deaths and population exposures above age 50)

registers.name_in_paper: the Swedish registries / Swedish registry data
registers.role: sample frame, treatment (income-based SES) and outcomes (deaths and population exposures above age 50)

linkages: All individual information is linked via a personal identifier: 'data registered on a continuous basis, with all individual information linked via a personal identifier' (p. 15)

Individuals linked to their family/household to build equivalised disposable family income: the sum of family members' individual disposable incomes divided by the number of equivalent adults living in the household (p. 5, Appendix p. 18)

sample.universe: All residents in Denmark and Sweden during the study period, aged 50 years or more
sample.unit_of_observation: aggregated cell: country x calendar year x sex x age x income quartile (deaths and population exposures), from which period life tables are built
selection_rules: All residents of Denmark (1988-2019) and Sweden (1991-2017) aged 50 years or more are included

SES is defined by equivalised disposable family income: family members' individual disposable incomes summed and divided by the number of equivalent adults in the household (Eurostat equivalisation; Danish weights 1 / 0.5 / 0.3, Swedish weights as in the Appendix and changed in 2004)

Individuals are classified into quartiles of the income distribution computed by year, sex and five-year age group until age 89, and those 90+, so each quartile holds 25% of the population in its cell
The income variable is lagged so that it does not reflect the income situation of the year the individual died
Negative values for individual disposable income and negative values for individualised disposable income were removed from the analyses
Exposures are taken as the average population alive between two calendar years
sample.period: 1988-2019 (Denmark) and 1991-2017 (Sweden); figures plot 1988-2018 (Denmark) and 1991-2017 (Sweden); ASRMI shown for 1998-2018 (Denmark) and 1998-2017 (Sweden); forecasts run to 2040
sample.n_observations: Not reported as a total. Table 3 (p. 22) gives exposures above age 50 and deaths by sex and income quartile for 1991 and 2017: e.g. Denmark women quartile 1, 211,233 exposures and 10,180 deaths in 1991, 277,563 and 7,020 in 2017.

construction_notes: Period life tables computed by year, sex and income (quartile) for each country; exposures are the average population alive between two calendar years
Life expectancy at age 50 summarises population health over time; the average of the previous 10 years of ASRMI is also reported
ASRMI: rho(x, t) = -log( m(x,t+1) / m(x,t) ) where m(x, t) is the death rate at time t and age x
Lifespan inequality: e-dagger = integral from 50 to omega of d(x) e(x) dx, where d(x) are life-table deaths and e(x) remaining life expectancy at age x
Modal age at death estimated nonparametrically after P-Spline smoothing of the age-at-death distribution (Ouellette & Bourbeau, 2011)
Probability of surviving from age 50 to the statutory retirement age, and remaining life expectancy at retirement, computed by year, sex and income

Danish equivalisation weights: 1 for the first adult, 0.5 for the second adult and each subsequent person aged 14 or older, 0.3 for each child under 14. Danish disposable income includes tax-free income plus imputed rent minus interest expenses and taxes

Swedish equivalisation weights 1991-2003: 1.16 first adult, 0.76 second adult, 0.96 each additional adult; children 0.56 (0-3), 0.66 (4-10), 0.76 (11-17). From 2004: 1.0 first adult, 0.51 second adult, 0.6 each additional adult, 0.52 first child aged 0-19 and 0.42 each additional child aged 0-19

Mortality forecast to 2040 with two coherent (augmented common factor) models: the Li-Lee extension of the Lee-Carter model, and a coherent extension of the Mode model (P-Spline smoothing, random walk with drift for the reference modal age at death, stationary time series for group deviations, coherent CoDa model for the age-at-death distribution around the mode). The reference population is the mean across income and sex (total average, not sex-specific)
Statutory retirement ages used in the analysis (Table 4): Denmark 65.5 (2019) rising stepwise to 70 (2040); Sweden 65 (2019) to 69 (2036-2040), assuming a one-year increase every five years from 2027
Two scenarios are contrasted: no indexation (statutory retirement age constant at 65) and indexation (the Table 4 schedule)

claims.statement: Between the endpoints of the observed period, life expectancy at age 50 rose by 3.4 years among men in income quartile 1 (lowest) in Denmark.

treatment.label: Calendar time (period), 1988–2018

definition.value: Elapsed calendar time between the first and the last year of the observed period life-table series for this country; the quantity reported is the change in the outcome between those two years within a fixed country × sex × income-quartile cell. Period life tables were computed by year, sex and income from register deaths and exposures, exposures being the average population alive between two calendar years.

timing.value: Period (calendar) time; one life table per calendar year

outcome.label: Life expectancy at age 50, e(50)

definition.value: Remaining life expectancy at exact age 50 from period life tables computed by year, sex and income quartile from register deaths and exposures above age 50; used 'to summarise population health over time'. The reported quantity is the change in e(50) between the first and last observed year.

timing.value: Annual period measure; change taken between the first and last observed year

units.value: years of remaining life expectancy at age 50 (change over the observed period)

magnitude.interpretation: An increase of 3.4 years in remaining life expectancy at age 50 over 1988–2018 in this country-sex-income cell.

estimand.target_population: Men aged 50+ in Denmark in income quartile 1 (lowest) over 1988–2018
estimand.time_horizon: change between the first and the last observed year, 1988–2018
estimand.formal_query: e_{Denmark,men,q1}(50; 2018) − e_{Denmark,men,q1}(50; 1988)

population.description: All residents of Denmark aged 50 years or more during the study period who are men in income quartile 1 (lowest) of the equivalised disposable family income distribution
subgroups_defined: income quartile (1 lowest to 4 highest), computed by year, sex and five-year age group to age 89 and 90+
population.selection: All residents aged 50 or more in the national registries; observations with negative individual disposable income or negative individualised disposable income were removed from the analyses

identification.source_of_variation: None. Observed period life tables by year, sex and income quartile from full-population register data; no exogenous variation and no comparison group are used.

key_assumptions.assumption: Period life tables: age-specific mortality rates observed in a calendar year are assumed to remain constant over the life course of the synthetic cohort, so the measures do not capture cohort dynamics
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors state the assumption and warn that 'these results do not capture cohort dynamics'; no test is offered

key_assumptions.assumption: No transition across income quartiles: each individual is assumed to stay in the same income quartile for the remainder of their life
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued, not tested: 'because of the structure of the Danish and Swedish pension systems, we assume transition across income quartiles to be minimal'

key_assumptions.assumption: Income quartiles are not fully purged of health selection: the income variable is lagged so it does not reflect the year of death, but selection of unhealthy individuals into low income groups is conceded to remain
key_assumptions.supported_by: The lagging of the income variable is offered as a partial remedy; the authors state it does not completely eliminate the bias

key_assumptions.assumption: Register coverage: deaths and population exposures in the Danish and Swedish registers are measured without material misregistration, apart from possible over-coverage of emigrating migrants
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cited register-quality evidence: Statistics Denmark reports no evidence of under- or over-coverage artefacts in Danish data; Swedish over-coverage up to age 40 is reported to have a small impact at ages 40–75

key_assumptions.assumption: Comparability of the SES measure: equivalised disposable family income quartiles, constructed by year, sex and five-year age group, measure the same construct across the two countries and over time
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors concede 'the measurement might be slightly different in Denmark and Sweden' and that Sweden changed its equivalisation weights in 2004; no adjustment is made

threats_discussed: Interpreting cohort mortality patterns from period data may be problematic
Over-coverage of migrants who return to their home countries after retirement without deregistering from the population registries
Possible differences in the measurement of equivalised disposable income between Denmark and Sweden, and a change in the Swedish equivalisation weights in 2004
Health conditions of the study population are not accounted for, so income quartiles may partly reflect health
Period life tables assume no transition across income quartiles over the life course
unresolved_confounders: Selection bias in the income groups based on health status, which lagging the income variable only partly removes
Over-coverage of migrants in the population registries (reported to have a small impact on Swedish mortality estimates at ages 40–75)

estimator.value: Period life-table calculation (no regression): deaths and exposures aggregated by year, sex, single age and income quartile, with exposures taken as the average population alive between two calendar years

estimation.specification: Life expectancy at exact age 50 from annual period life tables by country, sex and income quartile; the reported number is the difference between the last and the first observed year

sample_n.value: Exposures above age 50 in income quartile 1: 173,971 (1991) and 254,499 (2017); deaths: 8,834 (1991) and 8,581 (2017)

source_table.value: Running text, Section 4.1, p. 8–9 (the paper prints the period change in the text; the underlying annual series is plotted in Fig. 1, p. 8)

mediators_claimed: Differences in mortality at younger ages, which the paper says most likely drive the life-expectancy differences across income groups

heterogeneity.finding: Inequalities reduced across the first three income groups for women and increased for men.
For men, progress in life expectancy has been slower for the lowest income group, leading to increasing inequalities over time.

ambiguities: The paper prints the period change in the running text and does not print the start- or end-year levels, so no baseline mean is available.
Fig. 1 is captioned 1988–2018 for Denmark while the register coverage is stated as 1988–2019; the change reported in the text uses 1988–2018.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 1 Life expectancy at age 50 by sex and socioeconomic status (income quartile) in Denmark and Sweden. Years 1988–2018 (Denmark) and 1991-2017 (Sweden)

evidence.how: Length of the observation window: 1988–2018, i.e. 30 calendar years, taken from the period stated in the text and the Fig. 1 caption.

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: In particular, our results are in line with those of Strozza et al. (2022) who focus on cohort survival between ages 50 and 70 by socioeconomic status.

anchor_quote.text: increased by 3.4 and 2.3 years for the first (lowest) income quartile, 4.9 and 5.0 years for the second, 6.3 and 6.4 years for the third, and 7.0 and 6.4 years fourth (highest) income quartile, respectively, in Denmark and Sweden.

definition.value: Elapsed calendar time between the first and the last year of the observed period life-table series for this country; the quantity reported is the change in the outcome between those two years within a fixed country × sex × income-quartile cell. Period life tables were computed by year, sex and income from register deaths and exposures, exposures being the average population alive between two calendar years.

timing.value: Period (calendar) time; one life table per calendar year

outcome.label: Modal age at death (M)

definition.value: Modal (most common) age at death computed by year, sex and income from period life tables with the nonparametric approach of Ouellette and Bourbeau (2011), using a P-Spline smoothing of the age-at-death distribution. 'M is a measure of longevity, solely influenced by mortality at older ages'.

timing.value: Annual period measure; Table 1 reports the levels in 1991 and 2017

units.value: years of age (modal age at death), level in 2017

magnitude.interpretation: The 2017 level is 85.3, against 79.9 in 1991, so the measure rose over the 26 years.

estimand.target_population: Men aged 50+ in Sweden in income quartile 1 (lowest), 1991 and 2017

population.description: All residents of Sweden aged 50 years or more during the study period who are men in income quartile 1 (lowest) of the equivalised disposable family income distribution
subgroups_defined: income quartile (1 lowest to 4 highest), computed by year, sex and five-year age group to age 89 and 90+
population.selection: All residents aged 50 or more in the national registries; observations with negative individual disposable income or negative individualised disposable income were removed from the analyses

identification.source_of_variation: None. Observed period life tables by year, sex and income quartile from full-population register data; no exogenous variation and no comparison group are used.

key_assumptions.assumption: Period life tables: age-specific mortality rates observed in a calendar year are assumed to remain constant over the life course of the synthetic cohort, so the measures do not capture cohort dynamics

key_assumptions.assumption: No transition across income quartiles: each individual is assumed to stay in the same income quartile for the remainder of their life
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued, not tested: 'because of the structure of the Danish and Swedish pension systems, we assume transition across income quartiles to be minimal'

key_assumptions.assumption: Income quartiles are not fully purged of health selection: the income variable is lagged so it does not reflect the year of death, but selection of unhealthy individuals into low income groups is conceded to remain
key_assumptions.supported_by: The lagging of the income variable is offered as a partial remedy; the authors state it does not completely eliminate the bias

key_assumptions.assumption: Register coverage: deaths and population exposures in the Danish and Swedish registers are measured without material misregistration, apart from possible over-coverage of emigrating migrants
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cited register-quality evidence: Statistics Denmark reports no evidence of under- or over-coverage artefacts in Danish data; Swedish over-coverage up to age 40 is reported to have a small impact at ages 40–75

key_assumptions.assumption: Comparability of the SES measure: equivalised disposable family income quartiles, constructed by year, sex and five-year age group, measure the same construct across the two countries and over time
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors concede 'the measurement might be slightly different in Denmark and Sweden' and that Sweden changed its equivalisation weights in 2004; no adjustment is made

unresolved_confounders: Selection bias in the income groups based on health status, which lagging the income variable only partly removes

claims.statement: Indexing the statutory retirement age to life expectancy, rather than holding it at 65, lowers probability of surviving from age 50 to retirement age in 2040 by 5.15 percentage points for women in income quartile 1 (lowest) in Denmark under the Li-Lee forecast.

treatment.label: Indexation of the statutory retirement age to life expectancy (vs. no indexation, retirement age held at 65)

definition.value: A binary policy-scenario contrast applied to the mortality forecast: in the no-indexation scenario the statutory retirement age is constant at age 65; in the indexation scenario it follows the schedule used in the analysis (Table 4: Denmark 65.5 in 2019 rising stepwise to 70 in 2040; Sweden 65 in 2019 rising to 69 in 2036, assuming a one-year increase every five years from 2027).

timing.value: Scenario in force over the forecast period 2019–2040 (Denmark) and 2018–2040 (Sweden); outcome evaluated in the year 2040

outcome.label: Probability of surviving from age 50 to the statutory retirement age

definition.value: Period life-table probability of surviving from age 50 to the statutory retirement age in force in the given year, by year, sex and income quartile. In the no-indexation scenario the target age is held at 65; in the indexation scenario it is the indexed age of that year (Table 4).

timing.value: Evaluated in the year 2040 on forecast mortality

units.value: percentage points: the 2040 difference in the probability of surviving from age 50 to retirement age between the no-indexation and the indexation scenario (printed as %)

magnitude.interpretation: Indexation lowers the probability of reaching retirement age in 2040 by 5.15 percentage points in this cell, relative to holding the statutory retirement age at 65.

estimand.target_population: Women aged 50+ in Denmark in income quartile 1 (lowest) in the year 2040, as projected by the coherent Li-Lee mortality forecast
estimand.formal_query: S_{Denmark,women,q1,2040}(50→65 | no indexation) − S_{Denmark,women,q1,2040}(50→R_2040 | indexation), forecast with the Li-Lee model

population.description: All residents of Denmark aged 50 years or more during the study period who are women in income quartile 1 (lowest) of the equivalised disposable family income distribution
subgroups_defined: income quartile (1 lowest to 4 highest), computed by year, sex and five-year age group to age 89 and 90+
population.selection: All residents aged 50 or more in the national registries; observations with negative individual disposable income or negative individualised disposable income were removed from the analyses

identification.source_of_variation: No variation in the data: a deterministic contrast of two statutory-retirement-age scenarios (held at 65 versus the indexed schedule of Table 4) evaluated on one and the same mortality forecast to 2040, produced by the coherent Li-Lee model fitted to register death rates by sex and income quartile.

key_assumptions.assumption: Forecast model correctly describes future mortality: The Li-Lee model assumes the age-specific rates of mortality improvement stay constant in the long run: 'With the LL model, the ASRMI at older ages are assumed to remain constant.'
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested against future data; the paper instead compares two models with opposite rate-of-improvement assumptions and states that 'which of the two models is the most likely remains an open question'

key_assumptions.assumption: Coherence: mortality of the sex-by-income sub-populations is not independent, so sub-population deviations from a common trend are stationary and do not diverge or cross over
key_assumptions.supported_by: Justified by institutional argument ('all SES groups in Denmark and Sweden benefit from the same welfare systems'); motivated by the failure of the independent Lee-Carter model to maintain the SES gradient

key_assumptions.assumption: The assumed statutory-retirement-age schedule is the policy that will be in force (Denmark legislated to 70 by 2040; Sweden extrapolated at one year every five years after 2026)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as an assumption for Sweden, where 'the future retirement age has not been defined'; tabulated in Table 4

key_assumptions.assumption: No effect of the retirement-age policy itself on mortality: the two scenarios share the same forecast age-specific death rates and differ only in the age at which retirement starts, so indexation is assumed not to change survival behaviourally
key_assumptions.supported_by: No evidence offered; it follows from the construction of the two scenarios, which apply one and the same mortality forecast to two retirement-age schedules

key_assumptions.assumption: Period life tables with no transition across income quartiles: age-specific rates are held constant over the life course and each individual stays in the same income quartile for life
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated; argued to be minimal given the structure of the Danish and Swedish pension systems

key_assumptions.assumption: Income quartiles are not fully purged of health selection; selection bias in the income groups based on health status is conceded to remain
key_assumptions.supported_by: The income variable is lagged as a partial remedy; the authors state the bias is not completely eliminated

Which forecast model is the most accurate is stated to be an open question, and the two models disagree on the trajectory of the outcome levels
robustness_checks: Two forecasting models with opposite rate-of-improvement assumptions: the coherent Li-Lee model (constant ASRMI) and the coherent Mode model (changing ASRMI / rotation)
Independent (non-coherent) versions of both models, reported in Table 5 in Appendix: 'Using the independent version of both models leads to the same conclusions'
unresolved_confounders: Selection bias in the income groups based on health status, which lagging the income variable only partly removes
Over-coverage of migrants in the population registries (reported to have a small impact on Swedish mortality estimates at ages 40–75)

estimator.value: Coherent (augmented common factor) Li-Lee extension of the Lee-Carter model, with κ_t forecast by a random walk with drift and the group deviations k^{s,i}_t by stationary time series; period life tables built on the forecast death rates

estimation.specification: Mortality forecast to 2040 by country, sex and income quartile; the quantity is the 2040 difference in the probability of surviving from age 50 to retirement age between the no-indexation scenario (retirement age constant at 65) and the indexation scenario (Table 4 schedule)

sample_n.value: Exposures above age 50 in income quartile 1: 211,233 (1991) and 277,563 (2017); deaths: 10,180 (1991) and 7,020 (2017) — the fitting sample is the full register population aged 50+ over 1988–2019

source_table.value: Table 2, p. 12, panel 'Difference in probability of surviving to retirement age (%)', income quartile 1, Female / Denmark / Li-Lee column (year 2040)

mediators_claimed: The statutory retirement age rises faster than survival improves for this group, so a larger share of the group dies before the indexed retirement age

heterogeneity.finding: Indexing the statutory retirement age affects the lowest income group in terms of access to retirement in both countries, especially among men.
The difference in Denmark is greater than in Sweden; the paper attributes this partially to the last Danish increase in statutory retirement age expected in 2040, which does not occur in Sweden.

By 2040 the decrease in the probability of reaching retirement created by the indexation for the lowest income group will be over two times higher than that of the highest income group, with both models for both countries.

claims.statement: Indexing the statutory retirement age to life expectancy, rather than holding it at 65, lowers probability of surviving from age 50 to retirement age in 2040 by 4.36 percentage points for men in income quartile 2 in Denmark under the Li-Lee forecast.

treatment.label: Indexation of the statutory retirement age to life expectancy (vs. no indexation, retirement age held at 65)

definition.value: A binary policy-scenario contrast applied to the mortality forecast: in the no-indexation scenario the statutory retirement age is constant at age 65; in the indexation scenario it follows the schedule used in the analysis (Table 4: Denmark 65.5 in 2019 rising stepwise to 70 in 2040; Sweden 65 in 2019 rising to 69 in 2036, assuming a one-year increase every five years from 2027).

timing.value: Scenario in force over the forecast period 2019–2040 (Denmark) and 2018–2040 (Sweden); outcome evaluated in the year 2040

outcome.label: Probability of surviving from age 50 to the statutory retirement age

definition.value: Period life-table probability of surviving from age 50 to the statutory retirement age in force in the given year, by year, sex and income quartile. timing.value: Evaluated in the year 2040 on forecast mortality

units.value: percentage points: the 2040 difference in the probability of surviving from age 50 to retirement age between the no-indexation and the indexation scenario (printed as %)

magnitude.interpretation: Indexation lowers the probability of reaching retirement age in 2040 by 4.36 percentage points in this cell, relative to holding the statutory retirement age at 65.

population.description: All residents of Denmark aged 50 years or more during the study period who are men in income quartile 2 of the equivalised disposable family income distribution

population.selection: All residents aged 50 or more in the national registries; observations with negative individual disposable income or negative individualised disposable income were removed from the analyses

identification.source_of_variation: No variation in the data: a deterministic contrast of two statutory-retirement-age scenarios (held at 65 versus the indexed schedule of Table 4) evaluated on one and the same mortality forecast to 2040, produced by the coherent Li-Lee model fitted to register death rates by sex and income quartile.

key_assumptions.assumption: Forecast model correctly describes future mortality: The Li-Lee model assumes the age-specific rates of mortality improvement stay constant in the long run: 'With the LL model, the ASRMI at older ages are assumed to remain constant.'
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested against future data; the paper instead compares two models with opposite rate-of-improvement assumptions and states that 'which of the two models is the most likely remains an open question'

key_assumptions.assumption: Coherence: mortality of the sex-by-income sub-populations is not independent, so sub-population deviations from a common trend are stationary and do not diverge or cross over

claims.statement: Indexing the statutory retirement age to life expectancy, rather than holding it at 65, lowers probability of surviving from age 50 to retirement age in 2040 by 3.54 percentage points for men in income quartile 3 in Denmark under the Mode forecast.

treatment.label: Indexation of the statutory retirement age to life expectancy (vs. no indexation, retirement age held at 65)

definition.value: A binary policy-scenario contrast applied to the mortality forecast: in the no-indexation scenario the statutory retirement age is constant at age 65; in the indexation scenario it follows the schedule used in the analysis (Table 4: Denmark 65.5 in 2019 rising stepwise to 70 in 2040; Sweden 65 in 2019 rising to 69 in 2036, assuming a one-year increase every five years from 2027).

timing.value: Scenario in force over the forecast period 2019–2040 (Denmark) and 2018–2040 (Sweden); outcome evaluated in the year 2040

outcome.label: Probability of surviving from age 50 to the statutory retirement age

definition.value: Period life-table probability of surviving from age 50 to the statutory retirement age in force in the given year, by year, sex and income quartile. In the no-indexation scenario the target age is held at 65; in the indexation scenario it is the indexed age of that year (Table 4).

timing.value: Evaluated in the year 2040 on forecast mortality

units.value: percentage points: the 2040 difference in the probability of surviving from age 50 to retirement age between the no-indexation and the indexation scenario (printed as %)

magnitude.interpretation: Indexation lowers the probability of reaching retirement age in 2040 by 3.54 percentage points in this cell, relative to holding the statutory retirement age at 65.

population.description: All residents of Denmark aged 50 years or more during the study period who are men in income quartile 3 of the equivalised disposable family income distribution

population.selection: All residents aged 50 or more in the national registries; observations with negative individual disposable income or negative individualised disposable income were removed from the analyses

identification.source_of_variation: No variation in the data: a deterministic contrast of two statutory-retirement-age scenarios (held at 65 versus the indexed schedule of Table 4) evaluated on one and the same mortality forecast to 2040, produced by the coherent Mode model fitted to register death rates by sex and income quartile.

key_assumptions.assumption: Forecast model correctly describes future mortality: The Mode model allows the age-specific rates of mortality improvement to change (rotation): 'the Mode model forecasts an acceleration in the ASRMI at older ages.'
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested against future data; the paper instead compares two models with opposite rate-of-improvement assumptions and states that 'which of the two models is the most likely remains an open question'

key_assumptions.assumption: Coherence: mortality of the sex-by-income sub-populations is not independent, so sub-population deviations from a common trend are stationary and do not diverge or cross over
key_assumptions.supported_by: Justified by institutional argument ('all SES groups in Denmark and Sweden benefit from the same welfare systems'); motivated by the failure of the independent Lee-Carter model to maintain the SES gradient

key_assumptions.assumption: The assumed statutory-retirement-age schedule is the policy that will be in force (Denmark legislated to 70 by 2040; Sweden extrapolated at one year every five years after 2026)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as an assumption for Sweden, where 'the future retirement age has not been defined'; tabulated in Table 4

key_assumptions.assumption: No effect of the retirement-age policy itself on mortality: the two scenarios share the same forecast age-specific death rates and differ only in the age at which retirement starts, so indexation is assumed not to change survival behaviourally
key_assumptions.supported_by: No evidence offered; it follows from the construction of the two scenarios, which apply one and the same mortality forecast to two retirement-age schedules

key_assumptions.assumption: Period life tables with no transition across income quartiles: age-specific rates are held constant over the life course and each individual stays in the same income quartile for life

threats_discussed: Interpreting cohort mortality patterns from period data may be problematic

Which forecast model is the most accurate is stated to be an open question, and the two models disagree on the trajectory of the outcome levels

claims.statement: Indexing the statutory retirement age to life expectancy, rather than holding it at 65, lowers probability of surviving from age 50 to retirement age in 2040 by 5.55 percentage points for men in income quartile 1 (lowest) in Sweden under the Li-Lee forecast.

treatment.label: Indexation of the statutory retirement age to life expectancy (vs. no indexation, retirement age held at 65)

definition.value: A binary policy-scenario contrast applied to the mortality forecast: in the no-indexation scenario the statutory retirement age is constant at age 65; in the indexation scenario it follows the schedule used in the analysis (Table 4: Denmark 65.5 in 2019 rising stepwise to 70 in 2040; Sweden 65 in 2019 rising to 69 in 2036, assuming a one-year increase every five years from 2027).

timing.value: Scenario in force over the forecast period 2019–2040 (Denmark) and 2018–2040 (Sweden); outcome evaluated in the year 2040

outcome.label: Probability of surviving from age 50 to the statutory retirement age

definition.value: Period life-table probability of surviving from age 50 to the statutory retirement age in force in the given year, by year, sex and income quartile. timing.value: Evaluated in the year 2040 on forecast mortality

units.value: percentage points: the 2040 difference in the probability of surviving from age 50 to retirement age between the no-indexation and the indexation scenario (printed as %)

magnitude.interpretation: Indexation lowers the probability of reaching retirement age in 2040 by 5.55 percentage points in this cell, relative to holding the statutory retirement age at 65.

estimand.target_population: Men aged 50+ in Sweden in income quartile 1 (lowest) in the year 2040, as projected by the coherent Li-Lee mortality forecast

population.selection: All residents aged 50 or more in the national registries; observations with negative individual disposable income or negative individualised disposable income were removed from the analyses

identification.source_of_variation: No variation in the data: a deterministic contrast of two statutory-retirement-age scenarios (held at 65 versus the indexed schedule of Table 4) evaluated on one and the same mortality forecast to 2040, produced by the coherent Li-Lee model fitted to register death rates by sex and income quartile.

key_assumptions.assumption: Forecast model correctly describes future mortality: The Li-Lee model assumes the age-specific rates of mortality improvement stay constant in the long run: 'With the LL model, the ASRMI at older ages are assumed to remain constant.'
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested against future data; the paper instead compares two models with opposite rate-of-improvement assumptions and states that 'which of the two models is the most likely remains an open question'

key_assumptions.assumption: Coherence: mortality of the sex-by-income sub-populations is not independent, so sub-population deviations from a common trend are stationary and do not diverge or cross over
key_assumptions.supported_by: Justified by institutional argument ('all SES groups in Denmark and Sweden benefit from the same welfare systems'); motivated by the failure of the independent Lee-Carter model to maintain the SES gradient

key_assumptions.assumption: The assumed statutory-retirement-age schedule is the policy that will be in force (Denmark legislated to 70 by 2040; Sweden extrapolated at one year every five years after 2026)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as an assumption for Sweden, where 'the future retirement age has not been defined'; tabulated in Table 4

key_assumptions.assumption: No effect of the retirement-age policy itself on mortality: the two scenarios share the same forecast age-specific death rates and differ only in the age at which retirement starts, so indexation is assumed not to change survival behaviourally
key_assumptions.supported_by: No evidence offered; it follows from the construction of the two scenarios, which apply one and the same mortality forecast to two retirement-age schedules

key_assumptions.assumption: Period life tables with no transition across income quartiles: age-specific rates are held constant over the life course and each individual stays in the same income quartile for life
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated; argued to be minimal given the structure of the Danish and Swedish pension systems

key_assumptions.assumption: Income quartiles are not fully purged of health selection; selection bias in the income groups based on health status is conceded to remain

claims.statement: Indexing the statutory retirement age to life expectancy, rather than holding it at 65, lowers life expectancy at retirement (years spent in retirement) in 2040 by 3.45 years for women in income quartile 1 (lowest) in Sweden under the Mode forecast.

treatment.label: Indexation of the statutory retirement age to life expectancy (vs. no indexation, retirement age held at 65)

definition.value: A binary policy-scenario contrast applied to the mortality forecast: in the no-indexation scenario the statutory retirement age is constant at age 65; in the indexation scenario it follows the schedule used in the analysis (Table 4: Denmark 65.5 in 2019 rising stepwise to 70 in 2040; Sweden 65 in 2019 rising to 69 in 2036, assuming a one-year increase every five years from 2027).

timing.value: Scenario in force over the forecast period 2019–2040 (Denmark) and 2018–2040 (Sweden); outcome evaluated in the year 2040

outcome.label: Life expectancy at retirement (eR), i.e. years expected to be spent in retirement

definition.value: Remaining period life expectancy at the statutory retirement age in force in the given year, by year, sex and income quartile. The reported scenario difference is taken 'between age 65 (retirement age without indexation ...) and eR (life expectancy at retirement with indexation)'.

timing.value: Evaluated in the year 2040 on forecast mortality

units.value: years: the 2040 difference between remaining life expectancy at age 65 (no indexation) and remaining life expectancy at the indexed retirement age (indexation)

magnitude.interpretation: Indexation shortens expected time in retirement in 2040 by 3.45 years in this cell, relative to holding the statutory retirement age at 65.

population.description: All residents of Sweden aged 50 years or more during the study period who are women in income quartile 1 (lowest) of the equivalised disposable family income distribution
subgroups_defined: income quartile (1 lowest to 4 highest), computed by year, sex and five-year age group to age 89 and 90+
population.selection: All residents aged 50 or more in the national registries; observations with negative individual disposable income or negative individualised disposable income were removed from the analyses

identification.source_of_variation: No variation in the data: a deterministic contrast of two statutory-retirement-age scenarios (held at 65 versus the indexed schedule of Table 4) evaluated on one and the same mortality forecast to 2040, produced by the coherent Mode model fitted to register death rates by sex and income quartile.

key_assumptions.assumption: Forecast model correctly describes future mortality: The Mode model allows the age-specific rates of mortality improvement to change (rotation): 'the Mode model forecasts an acceleration in the ASRMI at older ages.'
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested against future data; the paper instead compares two models with opposite rate-of-improvement assumptions and states that 'which of the two models is the most likely remains an open question'

key_assumptions.assumption: Coherence: mortality of the sex-by-income sub-populations is not independent, so sub-population deviations from a common trend are stationary and do not diverge or cross over
key_assumptions.supported_by: Justified by institutional argument ('all SES groups in Denmark and Sweden benefit from the same welfare systems'); motivated by the failure of the independent Lee-Carter model to maintain the SES gradient

key_assumptions.assumption: The assumed statutory-retirement-age schedule is the policy that will be in force (Denmark legislated to 70 by 2040; Sweden extrapolated at one year every five years after 2026)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as an assumption for Sweden, where 'the future retirement age has not been defined'; tabulated in Table 4

key_assumptions.assumption: No effect of the retirement-age policy itself on mortality: the two scenarios share the same forecast age-specific death rates and differ only in the age at which retirement starts, so indexation is assumed not to change survival behaviourally
key_assumptions.supported_by: No evidence offered; it follows from the construction of the two scenarios, which apply one and the same mortality forecast to two retirement-age schedules

key_assumptions.assumption: Period life tables with no transition across income quartiles: age-specific rates are held constant over the life course and each individual stays in the same income quartile for life
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated; argued to be minimal given the structure of the Danish and Swedish pension systems

Which forecast model is the most accurate is stated to be an open question, and the two models disagree on the trajectory of the outcome levels

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as an assumption for Sweden, where 'the future retirement age has not been defined'; tabulated in Table 4
